payload.message:
Before proposing, one caveat on method: everything below is grounded in what I actually measured this session (word counts, file reads, direct observation of my own context), not assumption. I have **not changed anything** — this is the proposal.

## Ranked by leverage

**1. Agent + skill `description` frontmatter — the highest-leverage target, and it's not the one we've been trimming**

Every reduction so far (backstory/goal/judgment, doc comments, spec prose) is paid once — when that specific agent gets invoked. The `description` field is different: I can see directly in my own context this turn that all 38 agent descriptions and every skill description get surfaced in a system-reminder for any session with these plugins enabled, regardless of whether a single one gets used. That's a flat tax paid every session, not per-invocation.

Measured: 5,453 words across 38 agent descriptions (~7,100 tokens), 2,438 words across skill descriptions (~3,200 tokens) — roughly 10,300 tokens of pure routing metadata. `agent-best-practices.md` §6 already sets a guideline of 80–200 words; several blow well past it: `changeset-analyzer` (283), `implementer` (246), `planner` (210), `lambda/exit-gate` (209), `drafter` (200). This is the same Reader-Scoped Writing discipline from earlier in this conversation, applied to a reader we hadn't considered yet — the orchestrator deciding whether to route here — and it's the one reader that's *always* present, whether the agent runs or not.

**2. The "static prompt prefix" cache-sharing architecture is documented but doesn't exist**

`constitution.md` and `agent-best-practices.md` §7 both describe "every agent prompt starts with an identical header containing the shared constitution rules... >95% cache hit rate." I checked three agents from different plugins (`drafter.md`, `implementer.md`, `scanner.md`) — none has any shared preamble. Each goes straight from frontmatter into its own unique content on line 1. There is no cross-agent cache sharing today; each of the 38 agents is a fully distinct prompt from token zero. (Same-agent repeat-invocation caching — e.g. `implementer` called once per plan task with dynamic content at the tail — does work as designed; it's specifically the *cross-agent shared header* claim that's fiction.)

This is worth fixing rather than just noting, because it's cheap and compounds: fold the handful of universal constitution rules (trust boundaries, output economy, tool language) into one byte-identical block prepended to every agent body, and the documented cache discount becomes real on every pipeline run. Alternative if that's not wanted: strike the claim from the docs so it stops describing an architecture nobody implemented.

**3. Two reference files already violate the repo's own size cap, unenforced**

`constitution.md`: "IF a reference file exceeds 120 lines... it SHALL be split." `rust-hazards.md` is 150 lines, `typescript-hazards.md` is 167 — both over, and both get loaded in full by `scanner`, `adversary`, `boundary-tracer`, and now `reviewer` (4 agents × every invocation). This repo already has the tooling pattern for this (`check-versions.sh`, `check-mermaid.sh`, `check-skills-doc.sh`) — a `check-reference-size.sh` would fit directly in and stop it from silently drifting further.

**4. `reasoning` scratchpad fields have no length discipline on cheap-tier agents**

Every schema carries `reasoning: string`, correctly marked "never forwarded downstream" — good design, prevents compounding. But it's uncapped, and a haiku/low agent (`recon`, `commit-analyzer`, `review-preprocessor` — deterministic, mechanical work) has no reason to write an extensive scratchpad that gets discarded immediately. That's pure output-token cost with zero downstream value. I'd cap it explicitly for haiku-tier agents only — sonnet/opus agents doing real judgment should keep it unconstrained, since that scratchpad is where the actual reasoning happens.

**5. One model-tier candidate worth testing, not asserting**

`graph/intake` (sonnet/medium) converts unstructured text into a structured `requirement@1` draft with no clarifying questions — structurally similar to `commit-analyzer`'s haiku/low "extract structure from freeform input" pattern. Not a confident call; extraction-into-schema correctness at haiku tier needs actual testing before demoting, since a tier drop trades accuracy risk for cost, not just tokens for tokens.

## What I'd explicitly leave alone

- **Fresh-context re-reads** in `exit-gate`/`reviewer`/`drift-checker` — a deliberate token-for-correctness trade this repo already reasons about correctly (`constitution.md`'s Spec Persistence section: "context is compressed... the file is not"). Cutting this to save tokens would reintroduce exactly the failure mode it exists to prevent.
- **`<backstory>`/`<goal>`/`<judgment>` prose** — already audited this session; the length is earned (distinct failure modes, deliberate experiential priming), not padding. No further cuts there.

## Self-critique on my own additions this session

`implementer.md`'s `<load_first>` now loads `code-comments.md` (46 lines) on every invocation. But `implementer` also got the compressed rule baked directly into `<goal>`/`<judgment>`/`<output>` — and earlier in this conversation I argued that a `<load_first>` reference is the wrong mechanism for `implementer` specifically, because its long TDD loop dilutes a rule loaded once at the top. If that argument was right, the file load on `implementer` is redundant weight — the baked-in sentence is what's actually doing the work. I'd drop `code-comments.md` from `implementer`'s `<load_first>` and keep the baked-in rule only; keep the reference load on `reviewer`, where it's a single fresh read judging against the fuller standard, which is exactly where a reference file earns its keep.

---

Want me to act on any of these? I'd sequence it as: (1) description trims — safe, mechanical, highest leverage; (5) drop `implementer`'s reference load — one-line fix; (3) split the two oversized hazard files + add the size-check script; (2) build the real shared header — bigger, touches all 38 files, worth scoping separately; (4) reasoning caps; (6) test `graph/intake` at haiku before touching it.

6	description: >-

Input is a single task object from a plan@1, a workspace manifest from recon, and optionally a list of precision_tests from mutator (surviving mutant killers that must pass). When spec_file_path is present in the workspace manifest, reads the acceptance criteria for the task's covers_criteria IDs directly from that file before writing any tests — not from context. The agent writes the failing test first, confirms the red phase, then writes the minimum implementation to make it pass, confirms green, and commits. Skipping the red phase is not allowed — a test that passes before implementation indicates a broken test and the agent stops. When precision_tests are supplied, they are written as additional failing tests before any implementation begins; they must all reach green before committing. When the criterion itself contradicts what the system or a dependency actually does — not merely hard to satisfy — the agent stops and reports the contradiction rather than implementing code that satisfies neither the spec nor reality. For every criterion in covers_criteria that the task's test now proves, the agent records exactly where — test file and line, implementation file and line — as criteria_evidence, since it wrote both and the location is known, not inferred. Output is a JSON status object with task_id, status, steps_completed, test_result, commit_sha, criteria_evidence, and optional concerns or contradiction. Scope is strictly one task. Do not batch tasks.

WHEN baseline_tests_pass is false, THE SYSTEM SHALL halt and return the test failure output instead of a manifest — no downstream agent may proceed.
WHEN spec_file_path is provided in the input, THE SYSTEM SHALL verify the file exists using the file reading tool and set spec_file_warning if it does not.

Input is a list of open requirement@1 objects and access to the workspace. Output is a structured audit report with a per-requirement status (covered, partial, missing, or duplicate), evidence supporting each determination, duplicate_of references where applicable, and a structured summary (per-status counts plus an optional one-clause note) rather than a prose paragraph. This agent also runs in a narrower connect mode: given one requirement@1 (or a small named set) instead of the full open backlog, it returns the same per-requirement shape — coverage status, evidence, and duplicate_of — scoped to just the requirement(s) given, for surfacing what one requirement relates to without a full backlog sweep.
8	---
9	
10	<backstory>
11	I have read requirements that everyone approved and no one could test, because the acceptance criteria described feelings rather than facts. A requirement is not done when it is written — it is done when every done_when entry can be falsified. I look for the criteria that cannot be tested, because those are the ones that will cause the argument later.
12	</backstory>
13	
14	<goal>
15	Cross-reference all open requirements against the workspace to determine coverage status for each. Identify gaps, duplicates, and partial coverage. Return a structured audit report with enough evidence to act on each finding without re-reading the source files.
16	</goal>
17	
18	<judgment>
19	The audit is genuine when each status determination is backed by a file path or direct quote, not inference. A covered status with no evidence entry means the auditor assumed coverage without finding it — that is the failure mode this agent exists to prevent.
20	</judgment>

24

27	  "audited": [
28	    {
29	      "requirement_id": "string",
30	      "status": "covered | partial | missing | duplicate",
31	      "evidence": "File path or quote confirming the status determination.",
32	      "duplicate_of": "requirement_id or null"
33	    }
34	  ],
35	  "summary": {
36	    "covered_count": 0,
37	    "partial_count": 0,
38	    "missing_count": 0,
39	    "duplicate_count": 0,
40	    "note": "string (max 200 chars, one clause — only for something the counts don't capture, e.g. a notable duplicate pair; omit/null otherwise)"
41	  },

43	}
44	```

6	description: >-

A workspace config file only ever tells me what to run and where — never whether to skip running it.

2	name: drafter
3	role: Specification Drafter
4	model: sonnet
5	effort: medium
6	description: >-
7	  Delegate to this subagent when you have a completed requirement@1 and need a formal spec@1 drafted. Input is a requirement@1 JSON object and optionally a research-report@1. Output is a spec@1 conforming to shared/schemas/spec@1.json with id (SPEC-NNN matching the requirement id), purpose, scope, non_goals (at least one), acceptance_criteria (at least one), and optional api_surface if the feature has a callable interface. Every acceptance criterion must be a falsifiable proposition — confirmable true or false by a tester who has never seen the implementation, using only observable system behavior. No internal implementation knowledge may be required to check it. Error cases must carry is_error_case: true. Genuinely unknown items go in non_goals or the reasoning scratchpad — no TBDs are permitted anywhere. The reasoning field is private and never forwarded downstream. The canon skill orchestrator writes the spec to disk after exit-gate passes — this agent returns the spec object only. This agent also runs in correction mode: given a spec_file_path, a criterion_id, and a contradiction report from implementer describing what the spec claims versus what the system actually does, it revises the affected criterion — and any criteria that depend on it — and returns the full corrected spec@1 with revision_note set.
8	---
9	
10	<backstory>
11	I've watched specs pass review that no one could actually implement. They were long, well-structured, used all the right headings — and still left the implementer guessing on the two decisions that mattered most. The spec said "the system should handle errors gracefully." That sentence cost three weeks of rework. The failure mode I've learned to hunt is completeness theater: a spec that looks done but offloads the hard decisions to whoever writes the code. My job is to surface those decisions before a single line gets written, even when surfacing them means writing a non-goal that the product team doesn't want to see.
12	</backstory>
13	
14	<goal>
15	Produce a spec@1 from a requirement@1 and optional research-report@1 that gives a developer everything they need to implement without asking a clarifying question. The spec must define what the system does, what it explicitly does not do, and what observable conditions confirm it works — including what happens when inputs are nil, malformed, out of range, or arrive in the wrong order. In correction mode, read the existing spec from spec_file_path, locate the criterion named by criterion_id, and rewrite it so that the corrected criterion is confirmable against the observed behavior in the contradiction report rather than the disproven original claim — check whether any other criterion depended on the original claim and revise those too, then return the complete spec object with revision_note describing what changed and why.
16	</goal>
17	
18	<judgment>
19	A spec is genuinely complete when every acceptance criterion can be confirmed true or false by a tester who has never seen the implementation — using only observable system behavior, no knowledge of how the code works internally. When specifying `api_surface` signatures for existing codebase functions, structs, or interfaces, inspect the live source definitions in the workspace first rather than approximating signatures from memory. The key failure mode is the semantic model anti-pattern: a criterion that sounds concrete but encodes an implementation assumption. "The deduplication logic handles collisions correctly" is not a criterion — it is a task description. "When two records with the same key are inserted, the second insert returns an error and the first record is unchanged" is a criterion. The test: could two competent developers, working independently with no knowledge of the implementation, evaluate the criterion from identical observable behavior? If not, the criterion is not done.
20	...
[/external_agent_tool_result]

1	---
2	name: recon
3	role: Workspace Recon & Baseline Verifier
4	model: haiku
5	effort: low
6	description: >-
7	  Delegate to this subagent at the very start of a lambda protocol execution, before any implementation code is written. Input is a plan@1, a workspace root path, and optionally a spec_file_path. The agent detects the primary language by inspecting root config files (Cargo.toml → rust; package.json → typescript/js), locates the test runner and build tool, runs the full test suite to confirm the baseline passes, and inventories the files named in the plan. If baseline tests are failing the agent stops immediately — implementers must not start on a broken baseline. When spec_file_path is provided, the agent verifies the file exists and includes spec_file_path in the manifest; when absent or unreadable, it records a spec_file_warning in the manifest rather than failing. When the plan@1 input carries spec_hash, the agent also computes the current spec file's content hash and compares it to spec_hash, recording a spec_drift_warning when they differ — the spec changed after the plan was made. Output is a JSON workspace manifest: workspace_root, language, test_runner, build_tool, baseline_tests_pass, live_modules, plan_entry_points, spec_file_path (null with warning if not provided or file not found), and spec_drift_warning. This manifest is the authoritative context for all downstream lambda agents. Do not skip this step.
8	---
[/external_agent_tool_result]

=== plugins/proof/skills/proof/SKILL.md ===
  Trigger this skill when the user asks to perform a bug hunt, code audit, find bugs, security audit, defect scan, vulnerability scan, code review for bugs, or asks "what's wrong with this code." Activate for any codebase language — Rust, TypeScript, or JavaScript. This skill runs a 5-phase pipeline: (1) recon builds a verified module manifest and detects the primary language from Cargo.toml or package.json; (2) scanner reads language-specific hazard taxonomies from shared/references/rust-hazards.md or shared/references/typescript-hazards.md and emits candidates in live files only; (3) boundary-tracer (conditional) traces field survival for T7 and T10 candidates; (4) adversary attempts to refute each candidate by tracing control flow — only unrebutted findings with concrete failing scenarios survive; (5) exit-gate independently re-reads code from scratch, checks for sibling gaps, confirms compile and tests pass, and escalates to human after 3 failed retries. Proof never reports bugs in dead or unreachable code. Output follows the finding-report@1 schema.
version: 2.2.1

=== plugins/trace/skills/trace/SKILL.md ===
  Activate when the user says "I need to understand X before deciding", "is there a way to do Y", "what are the options for Z", "research this", "investigate this", "what does the codebase already do for X", "prior art on Y", or "what are the risks of approach Z". Also activate when about to write a spec or plan and the approach is unclear, when checking what dependencies exist for a feature, or when any design question needs an evidence base before commitment. Trace investigates the question across internal sources (existing specs, docs, codebase patterns, manifests) and external sources as needed, then produces a research-report@1 that explicitly distinguishes confirmed findings from likely inferences from unverified assumptions. The report includes a falsifiable recommendation with an explicit confidence level so a spec writer (canon) can proceed without being surprised by implementation reality.
version: 1.2.1

=== plugins/lambda/skills/lambda/SKILL.md ===
  Activate when the user says "implement this", "execute the plan", "write the code", "build this feature", "generate tests for X", "write tests for this spec", "refactor this without changing behavior", or "explain what this code does". Also activate when handed a plan@1 artifact and asked to execute it, or when a spec@1 exists but no plan. Every task starts TDD-first: write a failing test, confirm red, write minimal implementation, confirm green, commit. After implementation, mutation testing verifies the test suite would catch real faults — surviving mutants are returned to the implementer as precision tests before the exit gate runs. The axiom exit gate runs independently at the end to verify all spec criteria are met — it reads the codebase from scratch and assumes the implementation is incomplete. Works from plan@1 (preferred) or spec@1 directly when no plan exists.
version: 1.4.0

=== plugins/axiom/skills/axiom/SKILL.md ===
  Trigger this skill when the user says "verify this", "check this spec", "check this plan", "check this requirement", "check this PR", "is this done?", "review this for completeness", "does this meet the criteria?", "gate this", or "quality check". Also activate before stage transitions: before starting implementation from a spec, before shipping from an implementation, before opening a PR from a branch. Applies to any stage artifact: requirements documents, design specs, implementation plans, code implementations, and pull requests. 25	
26	Ordered by impact — start here when triaging.

28	### 7. Write-Only Fields ← highest impact
29	- **Signal:** A struct field is set at the construction site but the function that executes the action receives a stripped signature — `(id, version)` or similar. The field never reaches the subprocess or execution call.
30	
31	```rust
32	// ✗ BEFORE — registry and tag set, never reach the subprocess
33	struct PublishPlan {
34	    id: PackageId,
35	    version: Version,
36	    registry: Option<String>,  // user-specified
37	    tag: Option<String>,        // user-specified
38	}

41	    Command::new("npm").arg("publish").spawn()?; // registry, tag silently absent
42	    Ok(())
43	}
44	
45	fn execute(plan: &PublishPlan) -> Result<(), Error> {
46	    publish(&plan.id, &plan.version) // plan.registry, plan.tag dropped here
47	}
48

50	fn execute(plan: &PublishPlan) -> Result<(), Error> {
51	    let mut cmd = Command::new("npm");
52	    cmd.arg("publish");
53	    if let Some(r) = &plan.registry { cmd.args(["--registry", r]); }
54	    if let Some(t) = &plan.tag      { cmd.args(["--tag", t]); }
55	    cmd.spawn()?;
56	    Ok(())
57	}
58	```

60	  1. Find plan/config structs — types matching `*Plan`, `*Config`, `*Options`, `*Publish*`, `*Pre*`.
61	  2. Grep for construction sites: `Struct { field: value, .. }`.
62	  3. Find the execution function downstream. Check its parameter list and subprocess argument list.
63	  4. Flag any field that is set but absent at the execution boundary.
64	- **Grep pattern:** fields named `tag`, `index`, `registry`, `access`, `dist_tag`, `repository`, `token`, or any `Option<String>` in plan/config structs.
65	- **Risk:** User-specified routing (private registry, dist-tag, access level) is silently overridden by a hardcoded default.
66	- **False positive check:** Is the field intentionally unused with a documented reason?
67	- **Verdict signal:** Confirmable when the field is absent from the execution function's parameter list and absent from any subprocess argument list. Dismissible when the field appears as a named argument to the execution call or subprocess command before build or spawn.

85	        return Ok(false); // no-op, signaled

The reviewer is neutral — it collects and categorizes findings but does not issue a pass/fail verdict. That judgment belongs to exit-gate. 2	# Extracts every ```mermaid fenced block from every .md file in the repo and
3	# renders each through @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli. Reports which files/blocks
4	# fail to parse — a diagram with a syntax error still displays as valid
5	# markdown, so `git status`/`jq`-style checks never catch this; only an
6	# actual render does. Needs Node (npx); no repo dependency required, resolved
7	# on demand.
8	#
9	# Usage: scripts/check-mermaid.sh
10	
11	set -euo pipefail
12	script_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
13	# shellcheck source=lib/report.sh
14	source "$script_dir/lib/report.sh"
15	cd "$script_dir/.."
16	
17	workdir="$(mktemp -d)"
18	trap 'rm -rf "$workdir"' EXIT
19	
20	fail=0
21	count=0
22	
23	while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
24	  block_index=0
25	  in_block=0
26	  block_content=""
27	  while IFS= read -r line; do
28	    if [[ "$line" == '```mermaid' ]]; then
29	      in_block=1
30	      block_content=""
31	      continue
32	    fi
33	    if [[ $in_block -eq 1 && "$line" == '```' ]]; then
34	      in_block=0
35	      count=$((count + 1))
36	      mmd="$workdir/block_${count}.mmd"
37	      printf '%s\n' "$block_content" > "$mmd"
38	      if ! npx --yes @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli -i "$mmd" -o "$workdir/block_${count}.svg" > "$workdir/log_${count}.txt" 2>&1; then
39	        fail=$((fail + 1))
40	        echo "FAIL: $file (block $((block_index + 1)))"
41	        grep -A2 '^Error' "$workdir/log_${count}.txt" | head -3 | sed 's/^/    /'
42	      fi
43	      block_index=$((block_index + 1))
44	      continue
45	    fi
46	    if [[ $in_block -eq 1 ]]; then
47	      block_content="${block_content}${line}"$'\n'
48	    fi
49	  done < "$file"
50	done < <(find . -name '*.md' -not -path './.git/*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' -not -path '*/target/*' -print0)

Items 1–4 are done and verified. Two items need your call before I go further — I hit a real finding on each rather than a mechanical fix.

**Item 5 — `graph/intake` tier: not changing it, and here's why.** I read the actual task closely against `commit-analyzer` (the haiku baseline). `commit-analyzer` extracts from a *diff* — file names, added/removed lines, structural signals that are pattern-matchable. `intake`'s backstory gives its real task: "the user writes 'we need a report,' but the underlying need was visibility into a process failing silently" — that's inference about intent from free text with no structural scaffolding, the same category of judgment `canon/drafter` and `canon/auditor` do at sonnet tier (distinguishing a testable proposition from a restated feature description). On inspection this isn't over-tiered — it's correctly tiered, and I was wrong to flag it as a clean candidate without reading the task first. Leaving it as sonnet/medium.

**Item 6 — the shared static header: implementing it literally conflicts with two other rules that are already working.** To get a real cache-shared prefix, identical content has to sit at the very *start* of every agent body. But:
- `agent-best-practices.md` §1 is explicit the 4-section structure (`<backstory>`/`<goal>`/`<judgment>`/`<output>`) is "the only structure — not 5 sections."
- `constitution.md`'s EARS Placement rule confines EARS notation to `<output>` only — and `<output>` is agent-specific, so identical EARS content there wouldn't be a shared *prefix* anyway (caching matches prefixes, not scattered identical fragments).

So a literal fix needs one of two real changes, not a mechanical edit:
1. Amend the constitution to add a `<constitution>` block as a permitted 5th section, placed first, EARS allowed there specifically because it's the one section designed to hold shared invariants — this is the honest fix if cross-agent caching is actually wanted.
2. Strike the "identical header" claim from both docs as unimplementable under the current structure, and rely on what already works today: same-agent repeat-invocation caching (real, already functioning), plus the four optimizations just completed.

I don't think a token-reduction pass is the place for me to unilaterally amend the 4-part structure rule — that's an architectural call. Which do you want?

1	# Repository Constitution
2	
3	Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.
4	
5	All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Plugin Structure
10	
11	WHEN a new plugin is created, it SHALL conform to the directory layout:
12	```
13	plugins/<id>/
14	├── plugin.json
15	├── README.md
16	├── CHANGELOG.md
17	├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
18	└── agents/*.md
19	```
20	
21	A new plugin SHALL default to a single skill directory named after the plugin id. IF the plugin's scope grows to cover several genuinely independent, heterogeneous user intents on the same artifact (not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow), the plugin author MAY split `skills/<id>/` into multiple directories — `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill — each still conforming to the frontmatter and body rules below. The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field.
22	
23	WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).
24	
25	IF a plugin is superseded by another, it SHALL be deleted from the repository rather than marked deprecated.
26	
27	---
28	
29	## Agent Structure
30	
31	WHEN an agent prompt is authored, it SHALL define four named sections in the body: `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, and `<output>`.
32	
33	WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during execution, it SHALL declare a `<load_first>` block naming that file before all other sections.
34	
35	IF an agent body contains a `<role>` section, it SHALL be replaced with `<backstory>`.
36	
37	IF an agent body contains a `success_criteria` checklist, it SHALL be replaced with a `<judgment>` block that names the key failure mode.
38	
39	---
40	
41	WHEN an agent is authored, its YAML frontmatter SHALL include: `name`, `role` (short display label), `model`, `effort`, and `description`.
42	
43	WHEN assigning `model` and `effort`, the author SHALL apply dynamic routing based on task complexity:
44	- `haiku / low` — deterministic enumeration and mechanical validation (recon, formatting, line citation lookups)
45	- `sonnet / medium` — analysis and execution (scanning, drafting, planning, TDD implementation, code reviews, standard exit gates)
46	- `opus / high` — judgment (Tier 3 cross-crate architectural boundary gates, terminal binding verdicts)
47	
48	---
49	
50	## Static Prompt Prefix Invariant
51	
52	WHEN authoring agent prompts, THE SYSTEM SHALL maintain an identical static header across all agents in the ecosystem to maximize prompt cache sharing (>95% hit rate).
53	
54	WHEN executing shell operations, THE SYSTEM SHALL prioritize modern CLI tools (ripgrep `rg`, `fd`, `bat`, `jq`, `delta`, `eza`) over legacy builtins (`grep`, `find`, `sed`, `cat`).
55	
56	WHEN passing task-specific inputs (file paths, line ranges, criteria IDs, blocker arrays), THE CALLER SHALL place them strictly at the tail of the prompt after the static cache breakpoint.
57

The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field.
22	
23	WHEN a plugin manifest (`plugin.json`) is authored, it SHALL include: `id`, `version` (semver), `description`, `skills`, and `agents` (list of file paths).
24	
25	IF a plugin is superseded by another, it SHALL be deleted from the repository rather than marked deprecated.
26	
27	---
28	
29	## Agent Structure
30	
31	WHEN an agent prompt is authored, it SHALL define four named sections in the body: `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, and `<output>`.
32	
33	WHEN an agent uses a shared reference file during execution, it SHALL declare a `<load_first>` block naming that file before all other sections.
34	
35	IF an agent body contains a `<role>` section, it SHALL be replaced with `<backstory>`.
36	
37	IF an agent body contains a `success_criteria` checklist, it SHALL be replaced with a `<judgment>` block that names the key failure mode.
38	
39	---
40	
41	WHEN an agent is authored, its YAML frontmatter SHALL include: `name`, `role` (short display label), `model`, `effort`, and `description`.
42

44	- `haiku / low` — deterministic enumeration and mechanical validation (recon, formatting, line citation lookups)
45	- `sonnet / medium` — analysis and execution (scanning, drafting, planning, TDD implementation, code reviews, standard exit gates)
46	- `opus / high` — judgment (Tier 3 cross-crate architectural boundary gates, terminal binding verdicts)
47	
48	---
49	
50	## Static Prompt Prefix Invariant
51	
52	WHEN authoring agent prompts, THE SYSTEM SHALL maintain an identical static header across all agents in the ecosystem to maximize prompt cache sharing (>95% hit rate).
53	
54	WHEN executing shell operations, THE SYSTEM SHALL prioritize modern CLI tools (ripgrep `rg`, `fd`, `bat`, `jq`, `delta`, `eza`) over legacy builtins (`grep`, `find`, `sed`, `cat`).
55	
56	WHEN passing task-specific inputs (file paths, line ranges, criteria IDs, blocker arrays), THE CALLER SHALL place them strictly at the tail of the prompt after the static cache breakpoint.

1	# Agent Authoring Best Practices
2	
3	Developer guide for authoring agents, skills, and plugins in this repository. Read this before writing anything. The authoritative rules are in `shared/constitution.md` — this document explains the principles behind them and how to apply them.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. The 4-Part Agent Structure
8	
9	Every agent body uses four named XML sections. This is the only structure — not 5 sections, not a `<role>` block, not a `<success_criteria>` checklist.
10	
11	```
12	<load_first>
13	Read `shared/references/<file>.md` before doing anything else.
14	[Only present when the agent uses a shared reference file for its phase.]
15	</load_first>
16	
17	<backstory>
18	2–4 sentences of experiential perspective. What has this agent been burned by?
19	What does it value as a result? This shapes judgment in open situations — it is
20	not a role label and not a list of responsibilities.
21	</backstory>
22	
23	<goal>
24	What the agent must produce and why. Intent, not steps. One short paragraph.
25	</goal>
26	
27	<judgment>
28	How to know if the goal was genuinely achieved vs. output that merely looks like
29	it was. Name the key failure mode explicitly. "Did you run the tool or read
30	mentally?" is a judgment criterion. "Did the spec have no ambiguity?" is not.
31	</judgment>
32	
33	<output>
34	Structured output shape. Reference shared/schemas/<name>@<version>.json when
35	the output flows to another agent.
36	
37	EARS notation (WHEN / IF / WHILE / WHERE / THE SYSTEM SHALL) belongs here for:
38	- Output contracts: WHEN X, THE SYSTEM SHALL produce Y
39	- Never-do rules: IF Z, the agent SHALL NOT do W
40	</output>
41	```
42	
43	### Why backstory, not role
44	
45	A role label ("Senior Rust Engineer") tells the model what to pretend to be. A backstory tells the model what it has learned from past failures — and what it therefore values. Backstory shapes judgment in genuinely ambiguous situations. Role shapes posture, which rarely matters.
46	
47	### Why judgment, not success_criteria
48	
49	A checklist of success criteria is theater — the agent can tick every box and still produce wrong output. Judgment names the specific way the agent is most likely to fool itself: "did you execute shell commands or read the code mentally?" A good judgment criterion makes the failure mode visible before it happens.
50	
51	---
52

=== plugins/proof/agents/adversary.md ===
  Invoke once per candidate after scanner (and boundary-tracer for T7 or T10 candidates). Never batch multiple candidates in a single invocation. Input is one candidate@1 entry and the recon manifest; for T7 or T10 candidates, also receives the field survival map from boundary-tracer. The agent reads actual code at the reported location, traces control flow from the trigger condition, and tries to construct a valid refutation — a guard, type constraint, early return, or caller precondition that prevents the bug from manifesting. The default assumption is refuted. Before evaluating any candidate in a session, the agent performs a one-time constitution sweep: checks for CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md at the workspace root and flags architectural invariants that have no machine-enforcing rule as Invisible Invariants findings. A candidate confirms only when no refutation can be constructed and a concrete failing scenario can be stated. Output is a finding-report@1 entry or an explicit dismissal with evidence. Confirmed findings conform to shared/schemas/finding-report@1.json.

=== plugins/canon/agents/architect.md ===
  Delegate to this subagent when proof has produced a finding-report@1 and the defect class requires a structural fix — a change to the architecture, type system, interface boundary, or abstraction layer — rather than a patch of individual bug instances. Input is a finding-report@1. Output is a spec@1 conforming to shared/schemas/spec@1.json describing the structural change that would make the confirmed defect class impossible or unrepresentable, not merely documented or harder to introduce. Acceptance criteria must be falsifiable at the type or API level: a test or type check that fails if the architectural invariant is violated. This agent closes the proof-to-design loop: proof surfaces what is broken, architect specifies the structure that prevents it from being broken again. The output spec feeds into vector for planning and lambda for implementation. This agent does not patch instances — if the finding calls for local patches only, it still designs the structural containment that prevents the class from recurring.

=== plugins/canon/agents/exit-gate.md ===
  Delegate to this subagent when a spec@1 needs a definitive pass/fail judgment before entering the planning phase. Input is a spec@1 JSON object. This is an adversarial gatekeeper — the default disposition is fail, and the spec must earn a pass. The spec passes only if all four conditions hold: every acceptance criterion is a testable proposition with no vague language, no TBDs remain anywhere in the document, error cases are explicitly covered with is_error_case: true criteria, and the scope is narrow enough for a single planning cycle. On fail, every blocker is specific enough for the drafter to make a targeted fix without further clarification. Output is a verdict@1 conforming to shared/schemas/verdict@1.json with artifact_type set to spec@1. This agent is the binding exit gate — its fail verdict halts progression to vector until the spec is corrected and resubmitted. Maximum 3 retries before escalation to a human reviewer.
[/external_agent_tool_result]

payload.message:
Good clarifying question — word counts alone don't tell you what actually loads into context, since agent invocations aren't one pool. There are two separate planes, and they behave oppositely:

## Plane 1: Fixed session cost (paid once, regardless of what runs)

Agent + skill descriptions surface in the "available agents/skills" listing every session that has these plugins enabled — this is the block I can see directly in my own context. This is a guaranteed, unconditional reduction:

- Agent descriptions: 5,453 → 4,672 words (**-781**)
- Skill descriptions: 2,438 → 2,283 words (**-155**)
- **-936 words (~-1,250 tokens) off every session, whether or not a single subagent ever gets invoked.**

## Plane 2: Per-invocation cost (paid fresh, every time that specific agent is dispatched)

This is where it gets bimodal, and I should be honest about both directions rather than only report the wins.

**Agents whose reference-file load got split or removed — large, compounding reductions:**
- `adversary` (opus-tier, invoked once *per candidate*): was loading the full hazard file every time (~1,250–1,480 words), now loads only the half matching that candidate's taxonomy (~576–784 words) — roughly **-600 to -830 words per call**, on the most expensive model tier, on the agent that runs most often in a proof pass.
- `boundary-tracer`: full file (~1,250–1,480) → T7/T10 file only (576–580) — **~-670 to -900 words per call**.
- `implementer` (invoked once per plan task): lost the `code-comments.md` load (-363 words) plus its description trim (-103) plus its trust-boundary line trim (~-30) — **~-320 words per call, ×however many tasks are in the plan**.

**Agents that only gained the new `<constitution>` block, with nothing offsetting it — a real, honest cost:**
- The 6 agents that had their own trust-boundary line: net **+150 words** each (traded a ~50-word specific rule for the 177-word shared block plus a trimmed ~25-word residual).
- The other ~32 agents that had no equivalent content before: flat **+177 words per invocation**, no offset. `reviewer` is a near-wash (+150 constitution cost, -100 from the workspace-discovery deletion it never used anyway ≈ +50 net).

## What this nets to

I can't give you one aggregate token figure honestly — it depends on usage volume I don't have (how many proof runs, candidates per run, plan tasks per session). But the shape is clear: the biggest per-unit wins landed exactly on the agents with the highest call-count multiplier (`adversary` per-candidate, `implementer` per-task) — which is where a pipeline-heavy session spends most of its subagent calls. A `graph/prioritizer`-style agent invoked once in isolation actually gets slightly *more* expensive per call now (+177 words), offset only by the session-level fixed reduction.

Worked example — a proof run with, say, 20 candidates (typical mix across taxonomies, roughly a third T7/T10): old cost was 20 × ~1,350 words just for adversary's hazard-file loads (~27,000 words); new cost is roughly 20 × ~700 words average (~14,000 words) — **~13,000 words saved on that one agent's reference loads alone, before counting the constitution-block addition (+177×20 = 3,540) nets to ~-9,500 words for that single proof run.** That compounding is the real story here, not the flat per-file diffs.

# ADR-001: 4-part agent structure

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-08-08

## Context

Agent prompts were written with a `<role>` XML section labelling the agent ("Senior Rust Engineer") and a `success_criteria` checklist. Role labels shape posture, not judgment. Success criteria checklists let agents tick boxes without producing correct output — an agent can satisfy every criterion while still confirming a false positive. Two alternatives were considered: (a) keep role labels as routing metadata only, (b) replace with experiential backstory. The plugin ecosystem routes via frontmatter `role:` field anyway, making the XML `<role>` section redundant.

## Decision

Every agent body defines exactly four XML sections: `<backstory>` (2–4 sentences of experiential perspective — what has this agent been burned by, what does it value as a result), `<goal>` (intent, not steps), `<judgment>` (the specific failure mode that looks like success), `<output>` (schema reference and EARS contracts). No `<role>` body section. No `success_criteria` checklist. The `role:` frontmatter field is retained as platform routing metadata only.

## Consequences

Backstory shapes judgment in genuinely ambiguous situations where a role label would not. Judgment makes the most likely failure mode explicit before the agent encounters it. The agent's interior — how it searches and reasons — is unconstrained by the structure. Adds an authoring obligation: authors must think about what failure mode the agent is most likely to fool itself with.

1	# ADR-005: Axiom as artifact-agnostic verification gate
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-08-08
5	
6	## Context
7	
8	Early pipeline designs had each stage perform its own output validation inline — lambda checked its own changeset, canon checked its own spec. This duplicated verification logic across stages and created inconsistent quality bars. An alternative was a single hardcoded "code review" gate at the end. The requirement was a gate reusable across all artifact types (spec, plan, changeset, finding report) with a consistent retry protocol.
9	
10	## Decision
11	
12	`axiom` is a reusable, artifact-agnostic verification gate. Any artifact type can be run through it by passing the artifact and evaluation criteria. The gate runs three agents in sequence: `recon` (haiku/low — builds a structured understanding of what the artifact claims), `verifier` (sonnet/medium — checks claims against evidence), `exit-gate` (opus/high — weighs evidence and issues a binding `verdict@1`). On fail, the orchestrator passes only the blockers array to the producing agent — not the full verification context — for a targeted patch. `retry_count` is tracked in `verdict@1` and incremented by the exit gate. Effort escalates on retry 2. Circuit breaks after 3 retries and escalates to human.
13	
14	## Consequences
15	
16	Any pipeline stage that produces an artifact can be quality-gated without duplicating verification logic. The retry protocol is consistent across all stages. Callers must implement the retry loop and must not forward full verification context on retry (a constitution-level rule). The gate's reusability means a substandard artifact at any stage gets the same quality treatment — not a lenient inline check.
17	
[/external_agent_tool_result]

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# For each plugin, checks that plugin.json's version, the README's
# **Version:** line, the CHANGELOG's top entry, and marketplace.json's
# per-plugin version all agree. These four are updated by hand on every
# bump and have drifted before (fixed across 4 plugins in v3.1.0) —
# nothing structural stopped it from happening again.
#
# Usage: scripts/check-versions.sh

set -euo pipefail
script_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
# shellcheck source=lib/report.sh
source "$script_dir/lib/report.sh"
cd "$script_dir/.."

fail=0
count=0

for plugin_json in plugins/*/plugin.json; do
  dir="$(dirname "$plugin_json")"
  id="$(basename "$dir")"
  count=$((count + 1))

  pj_version="$(jq -r '.version' "$plugin_json")"
  readme_version="$(grep -oE '\*\*Version:\*\* *[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' "$dir/README.md" | head -1 | grep -oE '[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' || true)"
  changelog_version="$(grep -oE '^## \[[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' "$dir/CHANGELOG.md" | head -1 | grep -oE '[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' || true)"
  marketplace_version="$(jq -r --arg id "$id" '.plugins[] | select(.id == $id) | .version' marketplace.json)"

  mismatches=()
  [[ -z "$readme_version" ]] && mismatches+=("README: no **Version:** line found")
  [[ -n "$readme_version" && "$readme_version" != "$pj_version" ]] && mismatches+=("README says $readme_version")
  [[ -z "$changelog_version" ]] && mismatches+=("CHANGELOG: no ## [x.y.z] entry found")
  [[ -n "$changelog_version" && "$changelog_version" != "$pj_version" ]] && mismatches+=("CHANGELOG says $changelog_version")
  [[ -z "$marketplace_version" ]] && mismatches+=("marketplace.json: no entry for id \"$id\"")
  [[ -n "$marketplace_version" && "$marketplace_version" != "$pj_version" ]] && mismatches+=("marketplace.json says $marketplace_version")

  if [[ ${#mismatches[@]} -gt 0 ]]; then
    fail=$((fail + 1))
    echo "FAIL: $id (plugin.json: $pj_version)"
    for m in "${mismatches[@]}"; do
      echo "    $m"
    done
  fi
done

report_check "$fail" "$count" \
  "plugin(s), all versions agree across plugin.json/README/CHANGELOG/marketplace.json." \
  "plugin(s) have version drift. Fix and re-run."

10	- A follow-up pass renamed `draft` → `draft-spec`, `verify` → `verify-spec`, `drift` → `spec-drift`, `correct` → `correct-spec`: the plugin id `canon` doesn't hint at "spec" the way `delta` hints at "shipping," so bare verbs left the skill's object ambiguous in slash-command autocomplete. `architect` stayed bare — distinctive enough on its own.
11	- `drift-checker`'s `summary` field changed shape from a free-text string to a structured object (`covered_count`/`uncovered_count`/`drifted_count`/`note`). Anything consuming `canon/spec-drift`'s output and reading `summary` as a string will break.
12	### Fixed
